{"id": "42:28/q13", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "Mecca's seven-year drought or the Medinan Friday rain appeal; versions differ on the petitioner.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q13/p1", "position": "Rain was withheld from Mecca or Quraysh for seven years, then relief came.", "reasons": "Muqātil and transmitters give the Meccan drought. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports the Prophet's prayer lifted it after carrion and bones were eaten, with 44:15 an allusion; the Ibn Masʿūd account says the Prophet prayed for Joseph-like years after rejection and Abū Sufyān sought relief, while another Ṣaḥīḥ version records the prayer against Quraysh. Ibn ʿĀshūr infers a beginning around year eight, extending perhaps into nine."}, {"id": "42:28/q13/p2", "position": "The verse was revealed at the Prophet's Friday rain appeal prompted by a Bedouin.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī gives the Bedouin report. Ibn ʿĀshūr locates it in Medina during a Friday sermon; another version names the petitioner Kaʿb ibn Murra."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q14", "question": "What does يَنشُرُ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q14/p1", "position": "To spread, scatter, expand, or extend.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī contrasts nashr with folding, cites dispersed people and explains spread provision. Bursevī says spread or scatter. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the sense metaphorical expansion, citing 17:13. ʿĀʾisha's report of Abū Bakr restoring Islam's dispersed unity illustrates the usage."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q15", "question": "What is the mercy God spreads?", "turns_on": "Rain itself, its effects, all-encompassing mercy, or sun after rain.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q15/p1", "position": "The benefits of rain, including fertility, plants, fruit, and blessings across land and living creatures.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī name plants and fruit; al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī fertility; al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī plains, mountains, plants, animals. Al-Biqāʿī adds pools, rivers, trees, grain and fruit. Ibn Kathīr describes region and inhabitants; al-Jishumī says each person's benefit in each land. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it mercy through water; al-Māwardī notes general and particular reach. Abū Ḥayyān puts rain's benefits within broader mercy."}, {"id": "42:28/q15/p2", "position": "The rain itself, repeating and reinforcing the blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī cites 30:48, al-Baghawī 7:57; al-Dāmghānī groups 7:57, 25:48, 30:50, 30:36, 30:46 as rain usages. Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly calls this reinforcement. Al-Ālūsī finds the repeated blessing far-fetched."}, {"id": "42:28/q15/p3", "position": "God's broad mercy in all things, beyond this rain.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī give this alternative; Abū Ḥayyān says mercy is broader than rain; al-Ālūsī makes rain's effects one primary instance."}, {"id": "42:28/q15/p4", "position": "Sunlight after rain, a separate welcome blessing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya's group, Abū Sulaymān, al-Mahdawī, and Fatḥ al-Raḥmān say long rain becomes tiresome and sun welcome. Ibn al-Jawzī calls sun a seventeenth sense of raḥma. Al-Ālūsī rejects it as unsound."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q16", "question": "Whose mercy is meant by the pronoun in رَحْمَتَهُۥ?", "turns_on": "Whether the antecedent is God or, with one interpretation, rain.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q16/p1", "position": "God's mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī states this primary antecedent."}, {"id": "42:28/q16/p2", "position": "The rain's mercy or benefits.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī allows this antecedent under his rain-effects interpretation."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q17", "question": "What is conveyed by describing mercy as spread?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q17/p1", "position": "The breadth and distribution of divine benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says it shows complete power and subtle provision in each land; al-Biqāʿī extends its reach to water, landforms, and growth."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q18", "question": "What does ٱلْوَلِىُّ mean here?", "turns_on": "General care, ownership, special alliance, rain control, or spring rain itself.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q18/p1", "position": "The caring protector or benefactor who manages servants through grace.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī stresses beneficence; al-Ṭabrisī management and interests; al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī gracious care. Ibn Kathīr extends direction to this life and next. Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts beneficial protection with powerless idols. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls an ally one who does good to those under care; al-Biqāʿī says God is nearest in every matter."}, {"id": "42:28/q18/p2", "position": "The owner or master.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī lists this; al-Ṭabrisī includes ownership within guardianship; Bursevī calls Him master."}, {"id": "42:28/q18/p3", "position": "The ally, patron, or friend of believers and obedient servants.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Baghawī specify believers or obedient; al-Qurṭubī says He supports His friends; al-Kāshifī says He repairs believers' affairs by rain and kindness."}, {"id": "42:28/q18/p4", "position": "The controller who repeatedly sends rain.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports that wise rain reveals need, strengthens resolve, and answers distress."}, {"id": "42:28/q18/p5", "position": "Spring rain itself is called walī.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports a nondivine reading of both names."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q19", "question": "What does ٱلْحَمِيدُ mean here?", "turns_on": "Worthy of praise, actually praised, praising obedience, or spring rain itself.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q19/p1", "position": "God deserves praise for His acts, favors, and mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives 'deserving praise'; al-Ṭabrisī says all acts are kindness and benefit. Bursevī says He alone deserves praise, al-Biqāʿī every kind, Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to deliverance. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the names praise of beautiful action; Iṣlāḥī says rain displays His worthiness of praise and gratitude; Ibn Kathīr calls every outcome of decree praiseworthy."}, {"id": "42:28/q19/p2", "position": "God is praised by creation, the obedient, or every tongue for His favors.", "reasons": "Muqātil singles out rain; al-Ṭabarī names favors; al-Baghawī creatures; al-Rāzī forms of mercy; al-Nasafī obedient servants; al-Qurṭubī every tongue. Al-Māwardī pairs 'praised' with benefactor."}, {"id": "42:28/q19/p3", "position": "God praises obedient servants.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān offers this divine-name construal."}, {"id": "42:28/q19/p4", "position": "Spring rain itself is praiseworthy.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports that both closing descriptions may refer to spring rain."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q20", "question": "What is the form and voice of ٱلْحَمِيدُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q20/p1", "position": "The intensive faʿīl form with passive mafʿūl sense.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this morphology."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q21", "question": "Why end with ٱلْوَلِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q21/p1", "position": "The names fit deliverance: God cares for His charges and His gift merits praise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the pairing; al-Bayḍāwī connects care and mercy with praise; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it praise of beautiful action. Al-Biqāʿī connects patronage in 42:9 to rain as evidence of care."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q22", "question": "What spiritual reading is given to rain and renewed life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q22/p1", "position": "Mercy or inspiration revives hearts and renews repentance, remembrance, knowledge, intimacy, and nearness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ takes rain as mercy on saints' hearts, establishing repentance, return, watchfulness, care. Al-Qushayrī pictures withered spiritual time, obscured love and renewed inner life; his poem hopes estrangement ends, covenants revive, and a dry branch greens. Study Quran's Aj says inspiration revives hearts through remembrance and knowledge."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q23", "question": "What does the move between hope and despair teach inwardly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q23/p1", "position": "God exposes limitations in hope and comforts servants through His attributes in despair.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ describes this movement and reassurance; Bursevī cites the Mathnawī's calamity, supplication, intercession, and divine relief."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q24", "question": "What is reported about supplication during rain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q24/p1", "position": "It is answered or not rejected.", "reasons": "Thābit reports this and cites the verse; a Prophetic report pairs prayer under rain with prayer at the call to prayer."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q25", "question": "What reports describe rain's amount, source, and distribution?", "turns_on": "Heavenly route and measured drops versus constant annual total and moral redirection.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q25/p1", "position": "Rain is measured and descends from a sea beneath the Throne through heavens, with angels placing drops.", "reasons": "Bursevī relays Ibn ʿAbbās: the sea supplies animals; rain is strained; each drop has an angel, except the unmeasured Flood."}, {"id": "42:28/q25/p2", "position": "The annual amount is known to angels and unchanged, but sins divert rain to others or to deserts and seas.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports angelic knowledge and a hadith about redirection when some or all people sin."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q26", "question": "What does rain demonstrate about divine power and life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q26/p1", "position": "Its benefits and growth display God's power, sole divinity, and possibility of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī points to soft plants from hard soil and delicate branches from rough trees against resurrection denial. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees a sign of wondrous making and sole divinity; Iṣlāḥī calls it an everyday sign of God's action; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says blessings prove unity."}]}

{"id": "42:28/q30", "question": "How is hope, the opposite of despair, used in Arabic and the Qurʾan?", "turns_on": "Ordinary hope or contextual fear and lack of concern.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q30/p1", "position": "Rajāʾ normally means hope, including hope for God's mercy.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris distinguishes long-ā rajāʾ from short rajā, an edge or side, plural arjāʾ, citing 69:17. {"id": "42:28/q31", "question": "What makes praise truthful or excellent in poetry?", "turns_on": "Verified truth and benefit or imaginative range.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q31/p1", "position": "Truthful wisdom, counsel, and praise only for actual qualities make the finest poetry.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī reports moral distinctions and Zuhayr's truthful praise. He prefers this for sound reasoning, lasting effect, clear benefit, richer yield, and verification."}, {"id": "42:28/q31/p2", "position": "Imaginative untruth makes the finest poetry through figurative invention and exaggeration.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī reports the opposing view's broader craft in praise, blame, description, though he favors truthful poetry."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q32", "question": "What conventions of Qurʾanic wording and pairing are reported?", "turns_on": "Stable diction or paired concepts.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q32/p1", "position": "Recurring diction assigns stable senses or reference to certain words and addresses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr urges learning such patterns. Ibn ʿAbbās says Qurʾanic kaʾs means wine, also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and 'O people' means Meccan polytheists. Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna says Qurʾanic maṭar is punitive whereas ghayth here names rain."}, {"id": "42:28/q32/p2", "position": "The Qurʾan recurrently pairs related or opposed concepts.", "reasons": "Al-Jāḥiẓ lists prayer/almsgiving, hunger/fear, paradise/hell, hope/dread, emigrants/helpers, jinn/humans. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds benefit/harm and heaven/earth."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q33", "question": "Which passages of this sūra are reported Meccan or Medinan, and when was it revealed?", "turns_on": "Passage-level places and a tentative chronology from drought and Anṣār references.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q33/p1", "position": "The sūra is otherwise Meccan, with 42:23–24 reportedly about the Anṣār and 42:39–41 reportedly Medinan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes both exceptions to Muqātil and says the first belongs among Ibn ʿAbbās's four cited verses."}, {"id": "42:28/q33/p2", "position": "Revelation may have begun around year eight and continued into year nine.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr infers this from Muqātil's Meccan drought occasion for verse 28; he also suggests a post-ʿAqaba continuation since the Anṣār might be intended in 42:38 before Hijra."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q34", "question": "Where is this sūra placed in a reported revelation order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q34/p1", "position": "Sixty-ninth, after al-Kahf and before Ibrāhīm.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives al-Jaʿbarī's order from Jābir ibn Zayd."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q35", "question": "How many verses are counted in this sūra?", "turns_on": "Regional verse-counting traditions.", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q35/p1", "position": "Fifty.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes this to Medinan, Meccan, Syrian, and Basran counts."}, {"id": "42:28/q35/p2", "position": "Fifty-three.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes this to the Kufan count."}]}
{"id": "42:28/q36", "question": "What broader sūra themes frame this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:28/q36/p1", "position": "The sūra affirms revelation, divine rule and unity, provision, and judgment against idolatry.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says its disjointed-letter opening challenges deniers to match the Qurʾan; Muhammad's revelation resembles earlier revelation and warns Mecca; God owns heaven and earth, chooses human messengers, legislates. Study Quran describes wise distribution of wealth, offspring, revelation."}]}

{"id": "43:51/q10", "question": "What are the rivers?", "turns_on": "Whether literal Nile waterways or figurative commanders, wealth, or horses.", "positions": [{"id": "43:51/q10/p1", "position": "The Nile and its major branches or canals.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites commentators; Mawardi allows the Nile itself. {"id": "43:51/q19", "question": "How does the next 'am I better' relate to this question?", "turns_on": "Whether am connects, disconnects, means bal, receives a pause, or is redundant.", "positions": [{"id": "43:51/q19/p1", "position": "Am joins a balanced alternative: 'do you not see, or see I am better?'", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites Sībawayh and al-Khalil; Ibn Atiyya notes lā remains negative; Burhan acknowledges the connected parsing."}, {"id": "43:51/q19/p2", "position": "Am means bal, 'rather'.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, al-Suddi, Thalabi's majority, and a group cited by Ibn Atiyya."}, {"id": "43:51/q19/p3", "position": "Am is disjunctive and starts a new question.", "reasons": "Burhan calls this familiar and favored by the negative first question; al-Wahidi compares 52:42. {"id": "43:54/q04", "question": "What did their obedience to Pharaoh consist of?", "turns_on": "Whether obedience is described generally, as denial of Moses and affirmation of Pharaoh, or as a reported act in the pursuit.", "positions": [{"id": "43:54/q04/p1", "position": "They accepted Pharaoh's call to reject Moses and his message.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it obedience in denial; Ibn Ziyad in al-Mawardi says Pharaoh's speech moved them to deny Moses. {"id": "43:54/q05", "question": "Why did they obey Pharaoh so readily?", "turns_on": "The notes offer moral corruption, ignorance, fear, worldly authority, and the audience's recent wavering as explanations.", "positions": [{"id": "43:54/q05/p1", "position": "Their own wickedness and departure from God's obedience made them receptive.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites sinfulness and corruption; al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan cite wickedness; al-Nasafi says they had left God's religion. {"id": "43:54/q09", "question": "How is Pharaoh's domination read inwardly?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is applied to the commanding self's rule within a person or to purification from Pharaoh-like traits.", "positions": [{"id": "43:54/q09/p1", "position": "The commanding self dominates heart and spirit through desire and violations of religious law.", "reasons": "Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya, reported by Bursevi, says the self dominates the heart, spirit, and their attributes; obedience starts in fear and becomes willing as they absorb its traits."}, {"id": "43:54/q09/p2", "position": "One should purify the base traits seen in Pharaoh and Satan and seek divine guidance.", "reasons": "Bursevi reflects on what made Satan and Pharaoh what they became, urging purification before the return to God and praying for God's care and guidance."}]}
